title: Elihu Defends the Justice of God
summary: Elihu addresses the wise men listening and puts Job on trial before them. Job, he says, has claimed that God denied him justice and that it profits nothing to delight in God. Elihu answers that the Almighty cannot do wrong: he sustains every living thing by his breath, judges kings and nobles without partiality, sees every deed, and overthrows the wicked in his own time. He ends by declaring that Job speaks without knowledge and adds rebellion to his sin.
story: This is Elihu's second speech. In chapter 33 he spoke directly to Job, gently at first, arguing that God speaks through dreams and suffering. Now he turns to a wider audience, the wise men of the circle, and his tone hardens. His target is the charge at the center of Job's complaint: that God has treated an innocent man unjustly. Where the three friends defended God by accusing Job of hidden sin, Elihu defends God chiefly by describing who God is, the ruler of the whole world who has no reason to pervert justice. But by the end of the chapter he has joined the friends in condemning Job's words. The theme of God's greatness will grow through his last two speeches until God himself speaks from the storm in chapter 38.
historical:
The chapter has no fixed historical setting beyond the book's world of the patriarchal East. What stands behind it is a political ideal common to the ancient Near East: the ruler as guardian of justice. Kings across the region described themselves as defenders of the weak. The prologue to the laws of Hammurabi of Babylon (eighteenth century BC), for example, presents the king as appointed by the gods to make justice appear in the land so that the strong would not oppress the weak. Israel's own psalms and prophets expected the same of its kings and judged them by it.

Elihu applies that ideal to God himself, and raises it higher. Earthly kings owe their office to someone; God was appointed by no one (verse 13). Earthly kings favor the rich; God is not partial to princes. Earthly kings fall suddenly, sometimes in the night, and God is the one who removes them. The sudden deaths of the powerful, whether by plague, conspiracy, or battle, were a familiar feature of the ancient world, and Elihu reads them as God's judgment in action.
cultural:
Elihu frames his speech as a public hearing. He calls on the wise and learned to test what they hear, quoting a proverb Job himself had used (12:11): the ear tests words as the mouth tastes food. Disputes in the ancient world were often settled this way, by elders sitting together, hearing both sides, and choosing what was right. Elihu invites them to do exactly that with Job's case, and he casts Job almost as a defendant.

Several of his images come from court and palace life. To call a king worthless or a noble wicked to his face (verse 18) was unthinkable for a subject; only a higher power could do it. Clapping the hands (verse 37) was a gesture of scorn or defiance in that culture, the opposite of respectful silence before a superior. Elihu also charges Job with keeping company with evildoers (verse 8), which in a society built on honor and reputation was a serious accusation: a man was known by the company he kept.
literary: The speech is shaped as an argument in stages. Verses 2 to 4 summon the audience. Verses 5 to 9 state the charge by quoting or paraphrasing Job. Verses 10 to 30 form the long defense of God's justice, built on two main points: God's absolute sovereignty over creation (verses 13 to 15) and his impartial governance of rulers and nations (verses 16 to 30). Verses 31 to 33 pose a hypothetical, asking whether Job can dictate the terms of God's justice. Verses 34 to 37 return to the audience for a verdict against Job. Rhetorical questions carry much of the weight, and Elihu repeatedly uses the vocabulary of the lawcourt: justice, righteous, condemn, judgment.

outline.t: Elihu calls the wise to test his words
The charge: Job's claims against God
God cannot do wrong, and all life depends on his breath
The impartial ruler who judges kings and nobles
God sees every deed and overthrows the wicked
Job cannot set the terms, and his words lack insight

doctrines.note: Elihu grounds God's justice in his sovereignty. No one gave God charge over the earth; if he withdrew his Spirit and breath, all flesh would perish together. A God who owes his rule to no one and holds every life in his hand has no motive to act unjustly.

God repays each person according to his deeds and sees every step; no darkness hides evildoers from him. The Bible affirms this truth repeatedly, though the book of Job warns against assuming that the timing and form of that repayment can be read off a person's circumstances.
The chapter insists on God's righteousness and impartiality: he does not favor the rich over the poor, because all are the work of his hands, and he hears the outcry of the afflicted.

words.note: Mishpat, justice or judgment, the key word of the chapter. It can mean a legal decision, a person's right or case, or justice as a quality. Job had complained that God took away his mishpat, his right (verse 5). Elihu answers that the Almighty does not pervert mishpat (verse 12). The two men use the same word for a court case and for the character of the judge.

Shaddai, the Almighty, an ancient name for God used especially in Genesis and very frequently in Job. Its origin is uncertain; suggestions include a link to a word for mountain or to a word meaning to overpower. In this chapter it stresses God's supreme power in parallel with his justice (verses 10 and 12).

Evel, injustice or wrongdoing. Elihu uses it in verse 10 to deny flatly that the Almighty could act unjustly. The word is often used of dishonest dealings and corrupt judgment, which makes the denial pointed: God is not a corrupt judge.

Neshamah, breath. It is the word used when God breathes the breath of life into the first human in Genesis 2:7. In verse 14 Elihu imagines God gathering back his Spirit and breath, and all flesh returning to dust, an echo of Genesis 3:19. Life itself is on loan from God.

christ: Elihu's portrait of a ruler who is not partial to princes, who hears the cry of the poor, and who sees into every darkness is a portrait of God's justice that the rest of Scripture confirms and that the New Testament finds embodied in Jesus. The Gospels show him refusing to favor the powerful, welcoming the poor, and exposing hidden things. Yet the chapter also shows the limits of a courtroom approach to suffering. Elihu defends God's justice by condemning the sufferer. The New Testament holds God's justice just as firmly, but at the cross it shows the righteous judge taking the side of the condemned, and it names Jesus as the one in whom God is both just and the one who justifies (Romans 3:26). That connection is thematic, not a prediction in Elihu's words.

hard.q: Is Elihu fair to Job when he says Job claims there is no profit in delighting in God?
hard.a: Not entirely. In verse 9 Elihu puts in Job's mouth the claim that it profits a man nothing to delight in God. Job never quite said that of himself. He did describe the wicked as asking what gain there is in praying to the Almighty (21:15), and he did say that God destroys the blameless and the wicked alike (9:22). Elihu seems to have drawn Job's words together into their most damaging form. Some interpreters think this is fair summary: Job's protest, pressed to its logical end, implies that righteousness doesn't pay. Others see it as the same failure the friends showed, hearing a sufferer's anguish as blasphemy. Elihu is right that God does not pervert justice, and the book agrees. But the prologue has already shown that Job's faith was not a transaction; the whole test was whether he served God for nothing (1:9). Elihu's defense of God is sound in principle and mistaken in its verdict on Job.

questions: Elihu says that if God withdrew his Spirit and breath, all flesh would perish. How does it change your view of an ordinary day to believe that your life is sustained moment by moment by God?
God is not partial to princes and does not favor rich over poor. Where do you, or your church, tend to show the partiality God refuses?
Elihu defends God's justice but condemns Job in the process. How can we hold firmly to God's goodness without turning that conviction against people who are suffering?
